issues.legal_issue: Revenue courts have jurisdiction to decide whether an adoption is established when that question arises in a dispute over succession to a jagir.
material_facts: The dispute concerned succession to a jagir and whether the claimant had been adopted by its last holder.

The governing validation legislation assigned pending and future succession proceedings of this kind to the Revenue Courts, provided for appeals, made the Board of Revenue’s order final, and excluded civil-court jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The Board of Revenue was competent to decide the question of adoption.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 4, 5, 8, 12 and 13 of the Rajasthan Jagir Decisions and Proceedings (Validation) Act, 1955, validated and assigned jagir-succession proceedings to the Revenue Courts, provided for appeals and finality, and excluded civil-court jurisdiction over the specified proceedings.

predicates.jagir_succession_proceeding: The proceeding concerns succession to a jagir estate.
predicates.adoption_issue_in_succession: A party’s claim to succeed depends on whether an adoption occurred.

issues.definition: When a succession proceeding concerns a jagir and succession depends on whether an adoption occurred, the revenue forum may decide that adoption dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A supported factual finding of adoption by the Board of Revenue need not be reappraised on appeal when the Board has analyzed the evidence and there is no reason to revisit it.
material_facts: The Board of Revenue found that the claimant had been adopted by the last holder.
The record included oral evidence, an adoption deed, an invitation to the ceremony, and statements in an application seeking recognition of the adoption.
The Board carefully analyzed the evidence, and the authorities that had considered the issue had found the adoption proved.
issues.conclusion: The Board’s finding that the adoption occurred had to be accepted, and the Supreme Court declined to reappraise the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted a factual finding reached by the Board of Revenue after careful analysis of evidence that supported the finding, and saw no reason to reappraise that evidence in the appeal.

rule.if: appeal_from_revenue_fact_finding and tribunal_analyzed_adoption_evidence and record_supports_adoption_finding and no_reason_to_reappraise

predicates.appeal_from_revenue_fact_finding: The case is an appeal from a revenue tribunal’s factual finding.
predicates.tribunal_analyzed_adoption_evidence: The tribunal considered and analyzed evidence bearing on whether an adoption occurred.
predicates.record_supports_adoption_finding: The record contains evidence supporting the finding that the adoption occurred.
predicates.no_reason_to_reappraise: The appellate court identifies no reason to reappraise the evidence.

issues.definition: On an appeal from a revenue tribunal’s factual finding, if the tribunal analyzed the adoption evidence, the record supports its finding, and there is no reason to reappraise the evidence, the finding is accepted on appeal.

issues.legal_issue: The requirement of prior government sanction for recognition of an adoption under the Matmi Rules does not apply to an adoption made before those Rules were promulgated.
material_facts: The adoption was made before the Jaipur Matmi Rules were promulgated.
Rule 14(2) required prior government sanction for recognition of an adoption for succession to a state grant.
The State legislature later enacted a law validating the Matmi Rules, but that law did not give the Rules retrospective operation.
issues.conclusion: Rule 14(2) was prospective and did not require prior sanction for the pre-existing adoption.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 14(2) of the Jaipur Matmi Rules, 1945, is prospective. Section 2 of the Jaipur Matmi Rules (Validation) Act, 1961, deemed the Rules to have the force of law and to be existing jagir law for the specified enactments, but did not make the Rules retrospectively applicable to earlier adoptions.

predicates.adoption_predated_rules: The adoption occurred before the relevant succession rules were promulgated.
predicates.later_validation_did_not_make_rules_retr: A later validating enactment did not make the rules apply retrospectively to earlier adoptions.

issues.definition: If an adoption preceded the rules and a later validating enactment did not make them retrospective, the adoption does not require prior sanction under those rules.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court’s merits decision in a writ proceeding remains binding between the parties as res judicata despite a direction that the revenue tribunal decide the matter in accordance with the law declared by the High Court.
material_facts: In an earlier writ proceeding between the parties, the High Court considered the dispute on its merits and quashed the Board of Revenue’s order.
The High Court also directed the Board to decide the case in accordance with law and its observations.

The questions decided, expressly or by necessary implication, included the governing effect of personal law on succession and the inapplicability of the prior-sanction requirement to the earlier adoption.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s determinations were res judicata and could not be reopened before the Board or challenged in the appeal; the direction to decide in accordance with law did not make the merits determinations interlocutory.
issues.legal_principle: Questions expressly decided, or necessarily implied to have been decided, by a final merits determination between the parties are res judicata. A direction to a tribunal to decide in accordance with the law declared does not undo that effect where the court has quashed the tribunal’s order and determined the disputed questions.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: A later proceeding involves parties to an earlier judicial proceeding.
predicates.prior_writ_decided_questions_on_merits: In an earlier writ proceeding, the court decided disputed questions on their merits.
predicates.prior_order_quashed_tribunal_decision: The earlier court quashed the tribunal’s decision while directing it to act in accordance with the law declared.

issues.definition: When a later proceeding involves the same parties and an earlier writ court decided questions on the merits while quashing the tribunal’s decision, those questions are res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: Applying res judicata to bind a party to an earlier decision does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equal protection merely because a similarly situated person in another case might not be bound by that decision.
material_facts: The appellant argued that treating the High Court’s judgment as binding between the parties could result in different treatment of similarly situated persons.
The Court observed that the rule that pre-rule adoptions made according to personal law were valid applied to all such adoptions, while res judicata bound the parties to the earlier adjudication.
issues.conclusion: The application of res judicata did not violate the equal protection clause.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the equal-protection objection because applying res judicata did not single out a party for special or prejudicial treatment, and the stated rule concerning earlier adoptions applied generally to jagirdars in the relevant category.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge_to_res_judica: A party argues that applying res judicata in the case would deny equal protection compared with similarly situated persons.
predicates.party_bound_by_prior_adjudication: The party is bound in the case by an earlier adjudication between the parties.
predicates.general_rule_applies_to_similarly_situat: The substantive rule applied to the party is also applied generally to similarly situated cases.

issues.definition: When a party challenges res judicata on equal-protection grounds, is bound by an earlier adjudication, and the substantive rule applies generally to similarly situated cases, applying res judicata does not violate equal protection.
